flawed_step: Proof attempt: Step 1 is fine. Since the degree multisets are equal, there is a bijection f from V(G) to V(H) with deg_H(f(v)) = deg_G(v). Step 2 fails. It would need to show that some such bijection preserves adjacency and non-adjacency. Nothing in the definitions supports this, because the degree sequence only records how many neighbours each vertex has, not which vertices they are. The counterexample below shows that no bijection works.
counterexample: Let G = C6 on vertices {1,...,6} with edges 12, 23, 34, 45, 56, 61. Let H = two disjoint triangles on vertices {1,...,6} with edges 12, 23, 31, 45, 56, 64. Both are simple graphs with 6 vertices. Every vertex has degree 2 in both graphs, so both degree sequences are {2,2,2,2,2,2}. H contains the triangle {1,2,3}. G has no triangle: every edge of G joins an odd label to an even label, so G is bipartite, and a bipartite graph has no odd cycle. A bijection that preserves adjacency sends triangles to triangles, so the inverse of an isomorphism G→H would send the triangle {1,2,3} of H to a triangle in G, which is impossible. (Connectivity also separates them: G is connected and H is not.) So G and H are not isomorphic.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. C6 and two disjoint copies of K3 both have 6 vertices and every vertex has degree 2. They are still not isomorphic: C6 has no triangle and is connected, while 2K3 has triangles and is disconnected. The proof attempt breaks at the step that would need a degree-matching bijection to also preserve adjacency.
